issues.claim: The new product line is therefore squeezed into a few cells, which become huge (that explains the 100x lists and the latency jump: probing a big cell scans far more vectors), while queries in that region still probe only 16 lists, so many true neighbours sit in cells that are not probed (the new content is cut into more oversized cells than nprobe = 16 covers, along boundaries that were fit to the old data).
issues.problem: The correction created an internal contradiction: new content is 'squeezed into a few cells' yet also 'cut into more oversized cells than nprobe = 16 covers'. Executed check (faiss IVFFlat, 64-d, stale centroids trained on old data, new data added): when a few cells absorb the new content, recall at fixed nprobe goes UP (0.985 vs 0.881 for a freshly trained index at nprobe=4) while latency suffers. A recall drop needs the new region to span more oversized cells than nprobe probes, with old centroid boundaries cutting through new neighbourhoods. So the recall mechanism is stated as certain but is only true in that case.
issues.replacement: The new product line is therefore squeezed into a comparatively small set of old cells, which become huge (that explains the 100x lists and the latency jump: probing a big cell scans far more vectors). Recall falls when that region spans more oversized cells than nprobe = 16 can probe and the old centroid boundaries cut through the new neighbourhoods, so true neighbours end up in cells that are not probed; if only a few giant cells held the new content, skew alone would usually raise recall and cost latency, so measure recall per content type to see which case you are in.

difficulty_rationale: Subtle debugging: reconcile recall drop with latency rise and imbalance; fix/monitor.
